text.en: A dollar given with simcha counts as a thousand, more than a wealthy man's hundred dollars given with a grudge, so the same coin can be multiplied by how it is given.
The collector who interrupts davening may be the very present Hashem sends to save a person from distress he does not even know is coming.
The recession itself may be a test in tzedakah, sent to teach that when giving is harder it is even more important.
The killed shluchim have not ended their shlichus: from the heichal of Moshiach they should tell Moshiach the truth about the state of the Jews in India, as Avraham Avinu pleaded for the redemption.
Like a worm in a radish who thinks radish is the sweetest thing and cannot imagine a strawberry, people in this world cannot grasp the good of the next.
A person who never had to be rescued has a bigger miracle than one who brings a korban todah after being saved, for his miracle is that it never happened to him.
Yosef's 'I too will be carried up' was not selfishness at his father's deathbed: since a son's bones come from his father, carrying Yosef's bones was a hiddur in Yaakov's own burial.
Yosef said 'my bones' rather than 'me' precisely to show that he meant his father's part in him and the mitzvah, not his own person.
Yosef commanded his brothers and not his sons because the completion of Yaakov's burial belongs to Yaakov's sons before his grandsons.
'Yaakov Avinu did not die' belongs to the drush of Torah, which is read not in the Sefer Torah but in Jewish hearts, where Yaakov lives on.
The parsha in which Yaakov passes away is called Vayechi, 'and he lived', because Yaakov still lives in every Jew.
Melave Malka reaches higher than the Shabbos meals because after Shabbos the Jew lifts himself toward the Shabbos of the days of Moshiach, the future of David HaMelech.
'Too late' is said only of someone who died; since Yaakov did not die and no part of a Jew dies, no Jew is ever too late for teshuvah.
Because both Rosh Hashanah Torah readings fall in Parshas Vayera, the Mashgiach calls this Shabbos a rerun of Rosh Hashanah and a renewed time of pekidas akaros.
A man with twelve children can still be called barren if his Torah produces no chiddushim, for Torah is in a sense his wife.
The Mashgiach suggests a new reading of 'asher asah': the calf was made with Sefer Yetzirah, so it was not meat and serving it with milk posed no problem.
A calf made with Sefer Yetzirah is not halachically meat, since it does not descend from the first animals Hashem created, unlike a clone, which comes from an animal.
The angel revealed the Me'aras HaMachpelah at the very moment of Avraham's self-sacrifice for his guests, to show that Chava's future claim of discomfort was already answered measure for measure.

The parah adumah is a chok because it rests on Hashem's will, and Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael is likewise a will without reason, flowing from the souls being part of Him, as a mother's love flows from the child coming from her.
Shlomo HaMelech's 'and it is far from me' means that he wanted to become wisdom itself, as Moshe had become Torah itself, and this remained apart from him.
Moshe's humility was itself a chok: he did not try to understand why Hashem made him great, and so his root lay in the mitzvah of the parah adumah.
The staff with which Moshe performed his miracles hints that he saw himself as nothing more than a staff in Hashem's hand.

Hitting the rock is leadership as the king's messenger, in another's merit; speaking to it is malchus, ruling through speech in one's own merit, like Moshiach who will act through the breath of his lips.
Three consecutive parshiyos teach three levels of emunah: Shlach in Hashem, Korach in the tzaddik, and Chukas in oneself.
The parsha moves from the chok of the parah to the shirah because the lessons of emunah lead to shirah, preparing for the geulah as at the Yam Suf.

The Mashgiach reads 'zos chukas haTorah' to mean that parah adumah is the chok within the whole Torah: every mitzvah, even one we understand, has a dimension above understanding that draws from parah adumah.
The custom of traveling in Tammuz and Av is a rectification of the spies' forty-day journey, which spoiled emunah.
Rashi says Hagar 'strayed' back to idolatry rather than simply got lost, because for a believer there is no getting lost; only leaving emunah is called wandering.
Moshe struck the rock like a policeman with a stick instead of speaking like a king, because his humility would not let him act by his own merit once Miriam's merit was gone.
Building on Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch's pairing of Shelach and Korach, the Mashgiach adds that Chukas teaches a third emunah, belief in oneself.
The spies sent to Yazer succeeded where those of Shelach failed because they went with emunah and knew who sent them.

The physical spring and the days getting longer reflect a spiritual spring: Nissan is when the Jewish soul blossoms, and the Sefirah count, each day adding to the one before, mirrors daily growth toward Shavuos.

The Mashgiach shows that the content of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah is read in the Sefirah weeks, so the parshiyos themselves teach the 'purify us and sanctify us' of preparing for the Torah.
A bochur's yeshiva years are his private Sefirah, and the day he becomes a talmid chacham is his private Shavuos.
The requirement that the garment fit is written specifically by the lowliest avodah, because that is where a person is likely to feel the task is beneath him.
Greatness is measured by the ability to value small avodah; the bigger a person is, the more he understands the importance of a lesser task.
Bringing even fruitless trees into shul on Shavuos shows that one who did not reach the highest level but is content with his portion also has a share in the giving of the Torah.

The Mashgiach reads Adam and Chava's objection as a real claim of fairness: as the first owners of the cave they were entitled to privacy, like the halacha that a neighbor may demand a fence against being looked at.
Measure for measure in the law of fairness itself: one who sets aside his own comfort for guests loses the protection of others' comfort, so Avraham's hospitality is what opened the cave to him.
Taking Adam 'by the hand' means overcoming him with chesed, since in Chazal's language 'hand' stands for the attribute of chesed.
'Avraham will become a great nation' is the reason for revealing Sedom: a person who will leave behind a people serving Hashem has the status of the many, and his prayer works even after the decree.
In the name of the Yitav Lev: no prayer is lost. Avraham's unanswered prayer for Sedom was kept in reserve for his children, for in an emergency there is no time to start davening.
'We have a little sister and she has no breasts' describes a generation without mashpi'im, which must live on the remnants the great ones of the past left behind.
Chanamel's sale was a plan to keep the fruits of his field by trusting in Yirmiyahu's righteousness, but Yirmiyahu, knowing he was Shlomo's gilgul who caused the churban, took it as mockery.
'I am the G-d of all flesh' teaches that a reincarnated soul pays its old debt, but the new body is judged on its own and can be a tzaddik.
Korach's threat 'will you gouge out the eyes of these men' reveals that his men had once been the people of Sodom, who were struck with blindness.

Since only two cities may be burned as an ir hanidachas, Admah and Tzevoim were only overturned, and their remaining judgment of burning was carried out in Korach's eidah, which was both swallowed and burned.
Lot's living in a cave was a way of fulfilling the decree of Sodom in a mild form, the way going into the sukkah can stand in for a decree of galus.
Avraham had the water brought by a messenger because washing off the guests' idolatrous dust himself would have shamed them; his hatred of avodah zarah yielded to his chesed.
The same 'vayashkem Avraham baboker' appears when he sent away Yishmael and when he went to the akeidah, showing that his chesed was avodas Hashem and he could act against it when Hashem wished.

Hashem answered Yaakov's fear of Esav's two merits with Yosef, because Yosef became the tzaddik precisely when he was cut off from both his father and Eretz Yisroel; the Yehuda and Tamar episode shows the reverse.

Because kibud av lights up the attribute of Av above, Avimi, who kept it supremely, was shown that the churban was an act of a merciful Father, and the month of the churban is named Av for that reason.
Esav's outward kibud av, though empty, gives him a hold on the month of Av, which is why the churbanos of the Jewish people came in that month.
Esav excels in kibud av the way a pig shows its split hooves: what looks like his greatest virtue is exactly where his outwardness is exposed.
Both of Chazal's stories of gentile kibud av take place in Ashkelon, a Philistine city, because the Philistines descend from mamzerus and have no root, which exposes the hollowness of such honor.
Kibud av and yishuv Eretz Yisroel are the same mitzvah, honoring one's root, which is why the Torah gives kibud av the reward of length of days on the land.
The Chanukah light placed below ten tefachim is the Father bending down to His child, reaching into the deepest exile as Yosef's father's image reached him in Egypt.

Following Rabbi Dovid of Lelov, the place of hachnasas kallah in the list of birchos hashachar, right after visiting the sick and before what follows, shows that it rescues from what would otherwise come next.

The Mashgiach finds it significant that the Haiti earthquake came in the week of Parshas Va'eira, where Rashi teaches that Hashem's punishment of the nations is a lesson aimed at the Jews; so the disaster should be the headline of the Jewish papers.

Just as the Jews in Mitzrayim saw Hashem punish the Egyptians, took the lesson, did teshuvah and merited the geulah, so too now great plans for geulah are prepared in Heaven and all that is missing is that Jews take mussar.

Hachnasas kallah was chosen as the interruption because 'leshem yichud' shows that every mitzvah is meant to bring the Chassan, Hashem, together with the Kallah, Klal Yisrael; the purpose of all the mitzvos is itself a hachnasas kallah.

A collector who interrupts davening calling 'hachnasas kallah' should be thanked, because, as the Ba'al Shem Tov teaches that Hashem speaks to a person through everything he sees, he is reminding him that his davening itself must be a hachnasas kallah.
Fulfilling a mitzvah once in thought, speech and deed already completes that limb of the soul; the danger of gilgul is a limb never completed at all.
Klal Yisrael is itself one body with 613 parts: each Jew is a limb of it, the one who learns its head and the one who davens its heart, so a person shares in the mitzvos he himself cannot do.
Following Sefer Yetzirah's world, year and soul, the Mashgiach finds a 'tzaddik' in each: the tzaddik of the generation in souls, Yerushalayim in place, and Yom Kippur, together with Purim, in time.
The doubled 'achas bashanah' in the passuk alludes to two days that are really one: Yom Kippur and Purim.
'Doresh tov le'amo, vedover shalom lechol zar'o' refers not only to Mordechai's own generation but to all his spiritual descendants until today: he comes into every Jew's Purim.
Since Amalek attacked the weak ones at the rear, Purim, the victory over Amalek, belongs especially to the weak and simple; the great ones have Shavuos, Pesach and the Yamim Nora'im.
Without sod, pardes is missing a letter and becomes 'pered', a mule; a Jew must know that the Torah has an inner dimension and strive to reach it.

The Tanya calls Torah a garment, not food, because it is speaking of the mitzvah side of learning: in a mitzvah the act is the main thing and Torah accompanies it, while in learning Torah is the main thing and the mitzvah accompanies it.
The minhag that a tallis has no sleeves or shape for any limb reflects that tzitzis includes all the mitzvos, so its garment surrounds the whole body rather than a single limb.
That clothing costs more than food mirrors the spiritual order: Torah, the soul's food, is free and always available, while mitzvos, its garments, cost money and are not always at hand.
Learning Torah clothes a person twice: as a mitzvah that includes all 613, and through the mind itself, which is clothed in the Torah it grasps.
The burdens that kept the Rambam from writing more were Hashem's way of lengthening his life: had he been free, so great a masmid would have finished his measured portion of Torah while still young.
A soul's level of Torah does not alone set its greatness: a drop of wine is worth less than a barrel of orange juice, and the Beis Yosef was a giant soul of pshat, greater than a small soul of sod.

Parshas Parah falls on the last Shabbos of Adar, the lowest point of the year's order, because the parah is a tikkun for the lowest, which is why only its pshat and halachos can be learned; in this it is akin to Purim.
